tagline: Instantaneous speed is a limit not a reading
question_text: What does the dial actually measure?

audio_script: I am going to show you what a speedometer actually measures. Not a single reading, but a limit of many readings. Watch a ball fall. At the top the speed is zero. A fraction of a second later it is faster. Faster still. The graph on screen shows the same motion, drawn as a curve of position versus time. On that curve, the average speed over any interval is the slope of a secant line. Shrink the interval and the secant pivots. Shrink it again. In the limit, it becomes the tangent. The tangent slope is the instantaneous speed. Every dial is a derivative in disguise. The chain on the right is not the derivation of motion. It is the derivation of the derivative itself. Force equals mass times acceleration. Rearranged, acceleration is g. Integrate once and you get velocity. Integrate again and you get position. The live readout shows what the mathematical answer looks like as the ball falls. Everything in kinematics is built on this single limiting idea.

question_text: A hoop and a disk roll down the same ramp. Which wins?
audio_script: I am going to show you why the disk always wins. Same mass, same radius, same ramp. Release. The disk reaches the bottom first. Every time. Both lose the same potential energy. Both end with the same total kinetic energy. But kinetic energy has two flavours. Translational and rotational. For rolling without slipping, the rotational share depends on the moment of inertia. The hoop keeps its mass at the rim, far from the axis. Its inertia is the full m r squared. The disk spreads its mass out. Its inertia is only one half m r squared. A bigger fraction of the hoop's energy goes into spinning. Less is left for moving forward. The equation on screen morphs from the disk's formula to the hoop's formula to the inequality that follows. That single symbol change is the whole physics. Where the mass lives decides the race.

header_title: A Wave Is Not the Medium
tagline: The pattern travels while the particles stay put
question_text: Does the string travel with the wave?
audio_script: I am going to show you one of the most confusing ideas in wave physics. Pluck a string. A pattern travels from one end to the other. Now watch a single point on that string. It moves up and down. It does not travel. The wave is the pattern. The medium stays in place. The bottom graph shows this as an envelope over many small oscillations. Each crest and trough travels left or right, but the particles only bob. On the right, a Fourier sum builds a square wave from odd harmonics. That is not decoration. Every wave, no matter how complicated, is a sum of simple sines. The wave is the message. The medium is the messenger. And a pulse, like the gold one on screen, is a bundle of sines travelling together.

header_title: Blow Across a Sheet of Paper
tagline: Fast air pushes less. You would have guessed more.
question_text: Why does the paper rise?
equations_json: ["p+\\tfrac{1}{2}\\rho v^2+\\rho g h=\\text{constant}","A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2"]
audio_script: I am going to show you something that contradicts intuition. Hold a sheet of paper by its edge. Blow across the top. It rises. You expected it to sink. The reason is energy. A fast fluid element has more kinetic energy than a slow one. If nothing pushes energy in, pressure must drop. Pressure plus half rho v squared plus rho g h is constant along a streamline. Where the speed goes up, pressure goes down. Watch the venturi. The pipe narrows. Continuity forces the fluid to speed up. The gauge on the right shows pressure rising in the throat. Below, the hydrostatic tank shows how pressure grows with depth. Both are Bernoulli. Every atomizer, carburetor, curveball and wing uses this same fact.

audio_script: I am going to show you how one charge knows another is nearby. It cannot see. Yet bring two opposite charges together and they attract. Faraday gave us a way to think about this without action at a distance. Each charge creates something in the space around it. That something is the electric field. The colored lines on screen show the field of a dipole. The opacity map below shows the same thing numerically. Where the field is strong, the glow is bright. Where it is weak, the glow fades. In the middle, two vectors and their dot product show how two field contributions add. The warning box reminds you of the two rules every field diagram obeys.

tagline: Special relativity explains the magnetic force
question_text: Why do parallel currents attract?
audio_script: I am going to show you that magnetism is not a separate force. Two wires carry current in the same direction. They attract. Both contain moving electrons. Like charges should repel. So why do the wires pull together? Take the rest frame of the electrons in one wire. The other wire is not neutral in that frame. Length contraction packs the positive ions closer. Net charge imbalance. Electric field. Attraction. What we call magnetism in the lab frame, an observer riding on the electrons calls electricity. The compass needles on screen show the same field the wires produce. The coil below shows the same physics packaged for practical use. A cross product later, and you have the direction of the Lorentz force. Every magnet on your refrigerator is a relativistic artifact.

question_text: Why does heat flow one way?
audio_script: I am going to show you why you cannot un-stir coffee. Put a drop of ink in water. It spreads. It stays spread. Now try to gather it back into one corner. You cannot. Every collision between ink and water is reversible. But the number of ways to arrange the molecules in one corner is astronomically smaller than the number of ways to spread them out. The gas on screen is doing that calculation in real time. The random walk below is the same idea made visible. The integral and the rectangles to its right show the same bookkeeping in continuous form. Entropy counts arrangements. The second law is not a law of mechanics. It is a statistical near-certainty.

tagline: Light slows down in glass and bends
question_text: Why does a straw look broken?
audio_script: I am going to show you why a straw looks broken in a glass of water. Light slows down when it enters water. The speed of light in a medium is c over n. When light crosses a boundary at an angle, the change in speed bends the ray. Snell's law. Into a denser medium, the ray bends toward the normal. Out of one, away. The refraction on screen shows this in one continuous wave. The prism below bends each wavelength differently, which is why white light becomes a rainbow. The Michelson interferometer and the two-path diagram show the same idea in a different guise. Light takes two routes. Both routes are the same wavelength. When they recombine, they interfere. Every lens, every camera, every telescope is an application of the same physics.

question_text: Why do atoms emit only certain colours?
audio_script: I am going to show you why atoms emit only certain colours. Heat a gas. It glows. Not with a rainbow. With sharp lines. Bohr's answer was that the electron can only orbit at certain radii. Each orbit has a specific energy. Transitions emit a photon with energy equal to the difference. The atom on screen jumps inward. A photon flies out. The wave packet below shows a different quantum effect. A particle tunnelling through a barrier it does not have the energy to cross. Classically impossible. Quantum mechanically routine. The potential well and the wavefunction on the left show the same physics in a one-dimensional approximation. This is the ladder every chemistry student climbs.

question_text: Why do fast clocks run slow?
audio_script: I am going to show you how a proton crosses the galaxy in under five hundred years. At zero point nine nine nine nine nine c. The Milky Way is a hundred thousand light years across in its rest frame. On the proton's clock, only four hundred fifty years. The Lorentz factor is three hundred sixteen. From the proton's view, the galaxy contracts to three hundred twenty light years. It never breaks the speed of light. It takes a shortcut through spacetime. The curved grid on screen shows a related idea from general relativity. Mass warps space itself. The Taylor series to the right shows how special relativity reduces to Newtonian mechanics at low speeds. The same math, but only the first term survives. Every GPS satellite and every particle accelerator deals with this daily.

question_text: A one metre pendulum swings. What is its period?
audio_script: A pendulum one metre long. Period equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Plug in L equals one, g equals nine point eight. Two seconds. No mass. No amplitude. That is why pendulums were clocks for three centuries. Answer C.

question_text: A ball launches at 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Range?
audio_script: A ball launches at twenty metres per second, thirty degrees. Range equals v zero squared sine two theta over g. Sine sixty is about zero point eight six six. Twenty squared is four hundred. Divide by nine point eight. About thirty five metres. Answer B.

tagline: Conservation of momentum in one line
question_text: A 20 g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 500 g block. Block speed?
audio_script: A twenty gram bullet at three hundred metres per second hits a stationary five hundred gram block. Embeds. Momentum is conserved. Before, six kilogram metres per second. After, combined mass zero point five two kilograms. Six over zero point five two. Eleven point five. Answer B.

question_text: If the orbital radius doubles by what factor does the period change?
audio_script: Double the radius. Kepler says the period scales as r to the three halves. Two to the three halves is two root two. Answer C.

tagline: Energy leaks out of the oscillator
question_text: A spring with damping is released from amplitude A. How does the amplitude decay?
audio_script: A damped spring. The energy does not decay linearly. It decays exponentially. Every cycle loses a fixed fraction. Answer B.

question_text: Two identical slits are illuminated. What kind of pattern appears on the screen?
audio_script: Two slits. Two sources. The waves overlap. Where crests meet crests, bright. Where crests meet troughs, dark. Alternating bright and dark bands. Answer B.

tagline: Moving sources compress their own waves
question_text: A train whistle at 440 Hz approaches you. Is the observed frequency higher or lower?
audio_script: A train whistle at four hundred forty hertz approaches you. Higher or lower? The train moves toward you. Each crest launches from a closer position. Crests compress. Shorter wavelength. Higher frequency. Answer A.

question_text: Potassium has a work function of 2.0 eV. Below what wavelength does ejection stop?
audio_script: Potassium. Work function two electron volts. Threshold wavelength? h c over phi. Six point two four times ten to the minus seven metres. Six hundred twenty four nanometres. Answer A.

question_text: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between e and p?
audio_script: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between electron and proton. Plug in. Two point three times ten to the thirty nine. Answer C. And yet gravity runs the cosmos, because charges cancel and masses do not.

tagline: The period does not depend on speed
question_text: A proton at 5e6 m/s in a 0.5 T field. What is the period?
audio_script: A proton in a magnetic field of half a tesla. Period is two pi m over q B. Plug in. Six point six times ten to the minus eight seconds. Answer B. Notice the speed does not appear. Every proton takes the same time.

question_text: A wheel rolls without slipping. What curve does a point on the rim trace?
audio_script: A wheel rolls without slipping. A point on the rim traces a cycloid. Not a circle. Not a line. A cycloid. Answer D. The linear-algebra insets on the sides show that any smooth transform has this flavour of rotation plus translation.
